sentences.zh: 序

translations.literal: Preface.
translations.idiomatic: Preface.

sentences.zh: 夫帝王者，配德天地，葉契陰陽，發號施令，動關幽顯，休咎之徵，隨感而作，故《書》曰：「惠迪吉，從逆凶，惟影響。

translations.literal: As for emperors and kings, they match their virtue with Heaven and Earth, harmonize with yin and yang, issue commands and orders, and their acts bear upon both the hidden and the manifest; omens of blessing and calamity arise in response to stirrings; therefore the Documents says: "Follow the right path and there is good fortune; follow rebellion and there is ill fortune—like shadow and echo."
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign aligns his virtue with Heaven and Earth and moves in concert with yin and yang; when he issues orders, his influence reaches every realm, seen and unseen, and portents of weal or woe answer human conduct. Hence the Book of Documents: walk the straight path and you are blessed; walk the crooked path and you meet disaster—as inevitably as shadow follows form and echo follows sound.

sentences.zh: 」昔伏羲氏繼天而王，受《河圖》，則而畫之，八卦是也。

translations.literal: "In antiquity Fuxi succeeded Heaven and became king; he received the River Chart, took it as his model, and drew it—the Eight Trigrams are this."
translations.idiomatic: In high antiquity Fuxi received Heaven's mandate; the River Chart was revealed to him, and from its pattern he drew the Eight Trigrams.

sentences.zh: 禹治洪水，賜《洛書》，法而陳之，《洪範》是也。

translations.literal: Yu controlled the flood and was granted the Luo Document; he took it as law and set it forth—the Hong Fan is this.
translations.idiomatic: When Yu mastered the floods, Heaven granted him the Luo Document; he codified its teaching in the text we call the Hong Fan.

sentences.zh: 聖人行其道，寶其真，自天祐之，吉無不利。

translations.literal: The sage practices its Way and treasures its truth; Heaven blesses him of itself—auspicious; nothing is not favorable.
translations.idiomatic: When the sage upholds that Way and cherishes its truth, Heaven lends its aid, and every outcome turns fortunate.

sentences.zh: 三五已降，各有司存。

translations.literal: From the Three August Ones and Five Emperors downward, each had its office preserved.
translations.idiomatic: From the age of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors onward, each era retained its proper institutions.

sentences.zh: 爰及殷之箕子，在父師之位，典斯大範。

translations.literal: Down to Jizi of Yin, who stood in the office of royal father and tutor and presided over this Great Norm.
translations.idiomatic: This tradition reached Jizi under the Yin, who as royal instructor guarded the Great Plan.

sentences.zh: 周既克殷，以箕子歸，武王虛己而問焉。

translations.literal: When Zhou had conquered Yin, they brought Jizi back with them; King Wu emptied himself of self-importance and questioned him.
translations.idiomatic: After the Zhou overthrew Yin, they brought Jizi home from captivity, and King Wu humbled himself to seek his counsel.

sentences.zh: 箕子對以禹所得《雒書》，授之以垂訓。

translations.literal: Jizi answered with the Luo Document that Yu had obtained and imparted it to him as a legacy for instruction.
translations.idiomatic: Jizi replied with the teaching of the Luo Document that Yu had received, transmitting its lessons for posterity.

sentences.zh: 然則《河圖》、《雒書》相為經緯，八卦、九章更為表裏。

translations.literal: Thus the River Chart and Luo Document serve as warp and woof to each other; the Eight Trigrams and the Nine Sections alternate as outer and inner.
translations.idiomatic: The River Chart and Luo Document interlock like warp and weft; the Eight Trigrams and the nine divisions of the Hong Fan form an outer shell and inner core of meaning.

sentences.zh: 殷道絕，文王演《周易》；

translations.literal: The Way of Yin was cut off, and King Wen expanded the Zhou Changes;
translations.idiomatic: When Yin's mandate failed, King Wen elaborated the Zhou yi;

sentences.zh: 周道弊，孔子述《春秋》。

translations.literal: the Way of Zhou declined, and Confucius transmitted the Spring and Autumn.
translations.idiomatic: when Zhou rule decayed, Confucius compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals.

sentences.zh: 奉乾坤之陰陽，郊洪範之休咎，天人之道粲然著矣。

translations.literal: Upholding the yin and yang of Qian and Kun, offering at the suburban sacrifice the blessings and calamities of the Hong Fan—the Way of Heaven and man stands forth brightly manifest.
translations.idiomatic: He honored the cosmic polarity of Qian and Kun and presented at the suburban altar what the Hong Fan teaches about blessing and blame, so that the bond between Heaven and humanity stood forth in plain sight.

sentences.zh: 漢興，承秦滅學之後，文帝時，虙生創紀《大傳》，其言五行庶徵備矣。

translations.literal: When Han arose, inheriting after Qin's destruction of learning, in Emperor Wen's time Master Fu first compiled the Great Tradition to record it; his discussion of the Five Phases and the various omens was complete.
translations.idiomatic: After the Han rose from the wreckage of learning under the Qin, Emperor Wen's reign saw Fu Sheng compile the Great Tradition of the Documents, setting out the Five Phases and their prodigies in full.

sentences.zh: 後景武之際，董仲舒治《公羊春秋》，始推陰陽，為儒者之宗。

translations.literal: Later, between the reigns of Jing and Wu, Dong Zhongshu studied the Gongyang commentary on the Spring and Autumn and first extended yin and yang theory, becoming patriarch of the Ru scholars.
translations.idiomatic: Between Emperors Jing and Wu, Dong Zhongshu worked the Gongyang tradition of the Annals and pioneered yin-yang interpretation, winning recognition as the doyen of Confucian learning.

sentences.zh: 宣元之間，劉向治《谷梁春秋》，數其禍福，傳以《洪範》，與仲舒多所不同。

translations.literal: Between Xuandi and Yuandi, Liu Xiang studied the Guliang commentary on the Spring and Autumn, reckoned their blessings and calamities, and transmitted it with the Hong Fan—much of it disagreed with Zhongshu.
translations.idiomatic: Under Xuandi and Yuandi, Liu Xiang took up the Guliang Annals, correlated fortunes and disasters with the Hong Fan, and often parted company with Dong Zhongshu.

sentences.zh: 至向子歆治《左氏傳》，其言《春秋》及五行，又甚乖異。

translations.literal: When it came to Xiang's son Xin studying the Zuo Tradition, what he said about the Spring and Autumn and the Five Phases was again greatly at odds.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xin's scholarship on the Zuo Commentary produced yet another, sharply divergent reading of the Annals and the Five Phases.

sentences.zh: 班固據《大傳》，采仲舒、劉向、劉歆著《五行志》，而傳載眭孟、夏侯勝、京房、谷永、李尋之徒所陳行事，訖于王莽，博通祥變，以傳《春秋》。

translations.literal: Ban Gu relied on the Great Tradition, drew on Zhongshu, Liu Xiang, and Liu Xin to compose the Treatise on the Five Phases, and in the narrative recorded the deeds reported by such men as Sui Meng, Xiahou Sheng, Jing Fang, Gu Yong, and Li Xun down to Wang Mang—broadly encompassing auspicious anomalies to transmit the Spring and Autumn.
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu built on the Great Tradition and the three masters—Dong Zhongshu and the two Lius—to write the Han Treatise on the Five Phases, weaving in episodes cited by Sui Meng, Xiahou Sheng, Jing Fang, Gu Yong, Li Xun, and others down to Wang Mang, so that strange blessings and calamities illustrated the moral lessons of the Annals.

sentences.zh: 綜而為言，凡有三術。

translations.literal: Synthesizing them in one statement, in general there are three methods.
translations.idiomatic: Taken together, the doctrine falls under three heads.

sentences.zh: 其一曰，君治以道，臣輔克忠，萬物咸遂其性，則和氣應，休徵效，國以安。

translations.literal: The first says: when the lord governs by the Way and ministers assist with perfect loyalty, the myriad things each attain their nature, then harmonious qi responds, auspicious omens appear, and the state is thereby secure.
translations.idiomatic: First: when the ruler follows the true Way and his ministers serve with unstinting loyalty, creation thrives, harmonious energies gather, felicitous signs appear, and the realm rests at peace.

sentences.zh: 二曰，君違其道，小人在位，眾庶失常，則乖氣應，咎徵效，國以亡。

translations.literal: The second says: when the lord violates its Way, petty men hold office, and the multitude loses its norm, then perverse qi responds, ominous omens appear, and the state is thereby lost.
translations.idiomatic: Second: when the ruler abandons the Way, mean men fill office, and the people fall into disorder, malignant influences answer with ill omens and the state is undone.

sentences.zh: 三曰，人君大臣見災異，退而自省，責躬修德，共禦補過，則消禍而福至。

translations.literal: The third says: when the lord and great ministers see calamities or anomalies, they withdraw and examine themselves, blame their persons and cultivate virtue, jointly ward off and mend oversights—then disaster is dispelled and blessing arrives.
translations.idiomatic: Third: when ruler and high ministers heed prodigies, look inward, accept blame, reform conduct, and jointly correct faults, calamity yields and fortune follows.

sentences.zh: 此其大略也。

translations.literal: This is the general outline.
translations.idiomatic: Such is the outline of the theory.

sentences.zh: 輒舉斯例，錯綜時變，婉而成章，有足觀者。

translations.literal: Taking these examples and weaving them through the changes of the times, rounded and complete in pattern, there is enough in them worth observing.
translations.idiomatic: Applying these patterns across shifting ages yields a coherent narrative well worth study.

sentences.zh: 及司馬彪纂光武之後以究漢事，災眚之說不越前規。

translations.literal: When Sima Biao compiled events after Guangwu to complete the Han record, the doctrine of calamities did not overstep the prior model.
translations.idiomatic: When Sima Biao continued the Later Han narrative from Guangwu onward, his treatment of disasters stayed within the earlier framework.

sentences.zh: 今采黃初以降言祥異者，著於此篇。

translations.literal: Now I gather from the Huangchu reign onward those who spoke of auspicious anomalies and set them forth in this chapter.
translations.idiomatic: Here I collect records of omens and prodigies from the Wei founding (Huangchu) forward and present them in this treatise.

sentences.zh: 五行

translations.literal: Five Elements.
translations.idiomatic: The Five Elements.

sentences.zh: 《經》曰：「五行：一曰水，二曰火，三曰木，四曰金，五曰土。

translations.literal: The Classic says: "The Five Elements: first is called water, second fire, third wood, fourth metal, fifth earth.
translations.idiomatic: The classic text runs: "The Five Elements: first water, second fire, third wood, fourth metal, fifth earth.

sentences.zh: 水曰潤下，火曰炎上，木曰曲直，金曰從革，土爰稼穡。」

translations.literal: Water is called downward-soaking, fire is called upward-blazing, wood is called bending-and-straightening, metal is called yielding-and-changing, earth is called sowing-and-reaping."
translations.idiomatic: Water sinks and nourishes; fire climbs and burns; wood bends and straightens; metal yields to the forge; earth receives sowing and harvest."

translations.literal: Equals sign used as a typographical section divider.
translations.idiomatic: Typographical section divider.

sentences.zh: 木

translations.literal: Wood.
translations.idiomatic: Wood.

sentences.zh: =《傳》曰：「田獵不宿，飲食不享，出入不節，奪農時及有奸謀，則木不曲直。」

translations.literal: =The Tradition says: "If one hunts without lodging overnight, does not offer food and drink in sacrifice, comings and goings lack restraint, seizes farming seasons, or harbors treacherous plots, then wood will not bend and straighten."
translations.idiomatic: The commentary reads: "When rulers hunt without restraint, feast without ritual sacrifice, come and go without measure, disrupt the farming calendar, or plot treachery, wood loses its property of bending true."

sentences.zh: 說曰：木，東方也。

translations.literal: The explanation says: Wood is the east.
translations.idiomatic: The gloss runs: wood belongs to the east.

sentences.zh: 于《易》，地上之木為《觀》。

translations.literal: In the Changes, wood above earth forms the hexagram Guan (Observation).
translations.idiomatic: In the Zhou yi, wood resting on earth forms the hexagram Guan—Looking Down.

sentences.zh: 于王事，威儀容貌亦可觀者也。

translations.literal: As for affairs of kingship, deportment, bearing, and countenance are also things that may be observed.
translations.idiomatic: In governance, ritual bearing and personal presence are likewise there to be judged.

sentences.zh: 故行步有佩玉之度，登車有和鸞之節，三驅之制，飲食有享獻之禮；

translations.literal: Therefore in walking there is the measure of jade pendants; in mounting a carriage there is the harmony of carriage bells; there is the regulation of the three hunts; in eating and drinking there is the rite of offering and presenting;
translations.idiomatic: Hence measured pace with jade pendants at the belt, harmonized bells when mounting a chariot, the thrice-driven hunt, and at meals the proper rounds of offering and tasting;

sentences.zh: 出入有名，使人以時，務在勸農桑，謀在安百姓，如此，則木得其性矣。

translations.literal: going out and coming in have proper names; others are employed at the proper seasons; the task lies in encouraging farming and silkworms; the plan lies in securing the hundred clans—thus wood obtains its nature.
translations.idiomatic: comings and goings are regulated, labor is summoned in season, policy promotes tillage and silkworms, and planning aims at the people's welfare—then wood keeps its true nature.

sentences.zh: 若乃田獵馳騁，不反宮室；

translations.literal: But if one hunts and gallops and does not return to the palace chambers;
translations.idiomatic: But endless hunting and reckless riding that keep the ruler from his halls;

sentences.zh: 飲食沈湎，不顧法度；

translations.literal: if eating and drinking sink into dissipation without regard to statutes;
translations.idiomatic: gluttony and drunken heedless of law;

sentences.zh: 妄興徭役，以奪農時；

translations.literal: if corvée labor is rashly raised to seize the farming seasons;
translations.idiomatic: arbitrary corvée that steals the seasons of plough and weed;

sentences.zh: 作為奸詐，以傷人財，則木失其性矣。

translations.literal: if treacherous schemes are devised to harm people's wealth—then wood loses its nature.
translations.idiomatic: and treacherous schemes that strip the people of their substance—then wood forfeits its nature.

sentences.zh: 蓋工匠之為輪矢者多傷敗，及木為變怪，是為不曲直。

translations.literal: Thus craftsmen making wheels and arrows often meet spoilage, and when wood becomes monstrously transformed, this is "not bending and straightening."
translations.idiomatic: Wheelwrights and fletchers then find their timber spoiled, and when timber behaves monstrously, that is the fault called failure to bend straight.

sentences.zh: 魏文帝正月，雨，木冰。

translations.literal: In the first month of Wei Wendi, there was rain and trees were coated with ice.
translations.idiomatic: In the first month of Wei Emperor Wen's reign, rain fell and trees glazed with ice.

sentences.zh: 案劉歆說，上陽施不下通，下陰施不上達，故雨，而木為之冰，氛氣寒，木不曲直也。

translations.literal: According to Liu Xin's explanation, yang influence above did not penetrate downward, yin influence below did not rise upward; hence there was rain and the trees froze with ice—the vapors were cold—wood did not bend and straighten.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xin explained it thus: yang above failed to reach downward, yin below failed to rise; rain fell and sheathed the trees in ice—the air had turned bitter—so wood lost its quality of bending true.

sentences.zh: 劉向曰，冰者陰之盛，木者少陽，貴臣卿大夫象也。

translations.literal: Liu Xiang said: Ice is the flourishing of yin; wood is lesser yang and images noble ministers and grand officers.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xiang said ice marks yin at its height; wood stands for lesser yang and emblems high ministers and grandees.

sentences.zh: 此人將有害，則陰氣脅木，木先寒，故得雨而冰也。

translations.literal: When this person is about to suffer harm, then yin vapors press upon wood; first the wood grows cold; hence there comes rain and ice.
translations.idiomatic: When such a man is marked for harm, yin first grips the wood—the timber turns cold—so rain freezes upon it.

sentences.zh: 是年六月，利成郡兵蔡方等殺太守徐質，據郡反。

translations.literal: In that year in the sixth month, soldiers of Licheng commandery, Cai Fang and others, killed the prefect Xu Zhi and rebelled, occupying the commandery.
translations.idiomatic: That sixth month, troops in Licheng commandery led by Cai Fang murdered Prefect Xu Zhi and rose in revolt, holding the district.

sentences.zh: 太守，古之諸侯，貴臣有害之應也。

translations.literal: The prefect—among antiquity the feudal lords—was the response to harm coming to a noble minister.
translations.idiomatic: The prefect stood where ancient feudal lords once stood; the omen answered injury to a minister of rank.

sentences.zh: 一說以木冰為木介，介者甲兵之象。

translations.literal: One interpretation takes ice on trees as "wood armor," and armor is an image of weapons.
translations.idiomatic: Another reading treats glazed trees as "armored wood," armor being an emblem of arms.

sentences.zh: 是歲，既討蔡方，又八月天子自將以舟師征吳，戍卒十餘萬，連旌數百里，臨江觀兵，又屬常雨也。

translations.literal: That year they had already campaigned against Cai Fang; moreover in the eighth month the Son of Heaven personally led a naval expedition against Wu—more than a hundred thousand garrison troops, linked banners for several hundred li, reviewing troops along the river—and there was also persistent rain.
translations.idiomatic: The same year saw Cai Fang crushed; then in the eighth month the emperor took the fleet against Wu—well over a hundred thousand men, banners strung for hundreds of li, maneuvers along the Yangzi—and the rains still would not end.

sentences.zh: 元帝二月辛未，雨，木冰。

translations.literal: On xinwei day in the second month of Yuandi, rain and trees iced.
translations.idiomatic: On the xinwei day of the second month under Emperor Yuan, rain fell and the trees iced.

sentences.zh: 後二年，周顗等遇害，是陽施不下通也。

translations.literal: Two years later Zhou Yi and others met injury and death—this was yang influence not penetrating downward.
translations.idiomatic: Two years later Zhou Yi and his fellows perished by violence—yang failing to reach below.

sentences.zh: 穆帝正月乙巳，雨，木冰。

translations.literal: On yisi day in the first month of Mudi, rain and trees iced.
translations.idiomatic: On yisi in the first month of Emperor Mu, rain and glazed trees followed.

sentences.zh: 是年殷浩北伐，明年軍敗，十年廢黜。

translations.literal: That year Yin Hao campaigned north; the next year the army was defeated and he was dismissed for ten years.
translations.idiomatic: That year Yin Hao marched north; the next year his army was routed and he languished in disgrace for a decade.

sentences.zh: 又曰，荀羨、殷浩北伐，桓溫入關之象也。

translations.literal: It is also said: this was the image of Xun Xian and Yin Hao campaigning north and Huan Wen entering the passes.
translations.idiomatic: Some add that it foreshadowed Xun Xian and Yin Hao's northern campaigns and Huan Wen's thrust into the passes.

sentences.zh: 孝武帝十二月乙巳，雨，木冰。

translations.literal: On yisi day in the twelfth month of Xiaowudi, rain and trees iced.
translations.idiomatic: On yisi in the twelfth month of Emperor Xiaowu, rain fell and trees iced again.

sentences.zh: 明年二月王恭為北籓，八月庾楷為西籓，九月王國寶為中書令，尋加領軍將軍，十七年殷仲堪為荊州，雖邪正異規，而終同夷滅，是其應也。

translations.literal: The next year in the second month Wang Gong became defender of the north; in the eighth month Yu Kai became defender of the west; in the ninth month Wang Guobao became Palace Secretariat Director and soon added General of the Household Guards; in the seventeenth year Yin Zhongkan became governor of Jingzhou—though wicked and upright followed different courses, in the end they were alike extinguished; this was its response.
translations.idiomatic: The year after, Wang Gong took the northern frontier in the second month; Yu Kai the western frontier in the eighth; Wang Guobao became Palace Secretariat Director in the ninth and soon added command of the imperial guards; in the seventeenth year Yin Zhongkan took Jingzhou—wickedly inclined or loyal, they were all swept away in the end, matching the sign.

sentences.zh: 吳孫亮，諸葛恪征淮南，後所坐聽事棟中折。

translations.literal: Sun Liang of Wu: when Zhuge Ke campaigned against Huainan, afterward the main beam in the hall where he sat broke mid-span.
translations.idiomatic: Under Sun Liang of Wu, after Zhuge Ke's Huainan expedition the ridgebeam of his audience hall snapped at mid-span.

sentences.zh: 恪妄興征役，奪農時，作邪謀，傷國財力，故木失其性致毀折也。

translations.literal: Ke wantonly raised campaigns and corvée, seized farming seasons, devised evil plots, and wounded the state's resources—hence wood lost its nature and brought about splintering.
translations.idiomatic: Ke had launched needless wars and labor levies, stolen the farming seasons, spun wicked plots, and drained the treasury—wood therefore lost its nature and the timber gave way.

sentences.zh: 及旋師而誅滅，于《周易》又為「棟撓之凶」也。

translations.literal: When he turned the army back he was executed and destroyed; in the Zhou yi this is again "the disaster of a sagging ridgepole."
translations.idiomatic: When the army turned home he was put to death and his line cut off—the Zhou yi calls such a fate "the peril of the sagging ridgepole."

sentences.zh: 武帝五月，宣帝廟地陷，梁折。

translations.literal: In the fifth month of Wudi, the ground at Xuandi's temple sank and a beam broke.
translations.idiomatic: In the fifth month of Emperor Wu's reign the earth subsided at Emperor Xuan's temple and a beam cracked.

sentences.zh: 八年正月，太廟殿又陷，改作廟，築基及泉。

translations.literal: In the first month of the eighth year the Grand Temple hall again sank; they rebuilt the temple and piled the foundation down to the springs.
translations.idiomatic: The first month of the eighth year saw the Grand Temple hall sink again; they rebuilt the shrine, driving piles until they struck groundwater.

sentences.zh: 其年九月，遂更營新廟，遠致名材，雜以銅柱，陳勰為匠，作者六萬人。

translations.literal: In the ninth month of that year they finally built a new temple afar, importing celebrated timber and mixing in bronze pillars; Chen Xiu was master craftsman and sixty thousand laborers worked.
translations.idiomatic: That September they began a new temple complex, hauling in prized timber and setting bronze columns; Chen Xiu directed the work with sixty thousand hands.

sentences.zh: 至十年四月乃成，十一月庚寅梁又折。

translations.literal: Not until the fourth month of the tenth year was it finished; on gengyin day of the eleventh month a beam again broke.
translations.idiomatic: It stood finished only in the fourth month of the tenth year; that November another beam split on the gengyin day.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，地陷者分離之象，梁折者木不曲直也。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: sinking earth is an image of division; a broken beam is wood not bending straight.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven seemed to warn: subsiding earth betokens division; a snapped beam means wood no longer runs true.

sentences.zh: 明年帝崩，而王室遂亂。

translations.literal: The next year the emperor died and the royal house fell into chaos.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor died the next year, and the house of Jin slid into turmoil.

sentences.zh: 惠帝，成都王穎使陸機率眾向京都，擊長沙王乂，及軍始引而牙竿折，俄而戰敗，機被誅，穎遂奔潰，卒賜死。

translations.literal: Huidi: Chengdu Prince Ying had Lu Ji lead troops toward the capital to strike Changsha Prince Yi; when the army had barely moved the ceremonial pole splintered; soon they were defeated in battle, Ji was executed, Ying fled in rout and in the end was ordered to die.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Hui, Chengdu Prince Sima Ying sent Lu Ji toward the capital against Changsha Prince Sima Yi; the army had scarcely marched when the banner staff snapped; defeat followed quickly—Lu Ji was killed, Ying fled in rout, and was ultimately forced to kill himself.

sentences.zh: 此奸謀之罰，木不曲直也。

translations.literal: This was punishment for treacherous plotting—wood not bending straight.
translations.idiomatic: That was Heaven's rebuke for treacherous design—the fault of wood failing to bend straight.

sentences.zh: 元帝，王敦在武昌，鈴下儀仗生華如蓮華，五六日而萎落。

translations.literal: Yuandi: while Wang Dun was at Wuchang, flowers sprouted on the halberds of the guard like lotus blossoms; after five or six days they withered.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Yuan, while Wang Dun held Wuchang, lotus-like blossoms burst from the halberds of his escort; within five or six days they shriveled away.

sentences.zh: 此木失其性。

translations.literal: This was wood losing its nature.
translations.idiomatic: Wood had lost its proper nature.

sentences.zh: 干寶以為狂華生枯木，又在鈴閣之間，言威儀之富，榮華之盛，皆如狂華之發，不可久也。

translations.literal: Gan Bao took it that mad blossoms growing on dead wood, moreover within the bell pavilion, meant that the splendor of ritual display and the flourish of glory—all like these mad blossoms—could not last.
translations.idiomatic: Gan Bao read it as freak blooms on dead timber inside the bell pavilion: pomp and glory blazing up only to fade, no more durable than those unnatural flowers.

sentences.zh: 其後王敦終以逆命加戮其屍。

translations.literal: Afterward Wang Dun for rebellion finally had his corpse dishonored with execution.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun later rebelled and, dead, was dishonored on the corpse.

sentences.zh: 一說亦華孽也，于《周易》為「枯楊生華」。

translations.literal: Another explanation: this too was a flower prodigy; in the Zhou yi it is "a withered poplar putting forth blossoms."
translations.idiomatic: Another view calls it a floral anomaly—the Zhou yi speaks of "withered willows sending forth blossoms."

sentences.zh: 桓玄始篡，龍旂竿折。

translations.literal: When Huan Xuan first usurped, the dragon-banner pole snapped.
translations.idiomatic: When Huan Xuan began his usurpation, the dragon-banner staff broke.

sentences.zh: 時玄田獵無度，飲食奢恣，土木妨農，又多奸謀，故木失其性。

translations.literal: At that time Xuan hunted without limit, ate and drank extravagantly, earthworks harmed farming, and there were many treacherous plots—hence wood lost its nature.
translations.idiomatic: He hunted without restraint, feasted recklessly, poured labor into works that stole farmers from the fields, and spun endless intrigue—wood therefore lost its nature.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，旂所以掛三辰，章著明也，旂竿之折，高明去矣。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: the banner is what hangs the three luminaries and makes brilliance manifest; when the banner pole snaps, the high and bright are gone.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven's warning: the standard displays the three luminaries and proclaims authority—snap the staff and the high splendor departs.

sentences.zh: 玄果敗。

translations.literal: In the end Xuan was defeated.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan was indeed destroyed.

translations.literal: Equals sign used as a typographical section divider.
translations.idiomatic: Typographical section divider.

sentences.zh: 火

translations.literal: Fire.
translations.idiomatic: Fire.

sentences.zh: =《傳》：「棄法津，逐功臣，殺太子，以妾為妻，則火不炎上。」

translations.literal: =The Tradition: "If one casts aside the laws and fords, drives away meritorious ministers, kills the heir apparent, and takes a concubine as wife, then fire will not blaze upward."
translations.idiomatic: The commentary states: "Neglect law and duty, banish those who built your throne, murder the heir, and elevate a concubine to wife—then fire will not rise as it should."

sentences.zh: 說曰：火，南方，揚光輝為明者也。

translations.literal: The explanation says: Fire is the south; it raises radiance and is what brings brightness.
translations.idiomatic: The gloss: fire is the south, the force that lifts radiance into clear light.

sentences.zh: 其于王者，南面向明而治。

translations.literal: As for the kingly person, he faces south toward the light and governs.
translations.idiomatic: The true king faces south into the light and there holds court.

sentences.zh: 《書》云：「知人則哲，能官人。

translations.literal: The Documents says: "To know men is to be wise and able to assign them office.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Documents says: "To know your men is wisdom; that wisdom lets you place them in office."

sentences.zh: 」故堯舜舉群賢而命之朝，遠四佞而放諸野。

translations.literal: "Hence Yao and Shun raised the host of worthies and charged them to court, banished the four wicked ones far into the wilderness.
translations.idiomatic: Hence Yao and Shun filled court with the worthy and drove the four villains to the wilds."

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「浸潤之譖，膚受之訴，不行焉，可謂明矣。

translations.literal: Confucius said: "Insidious slander that soaks in and appeal that strikes the skin—if these do not prevail, one may be called enlightened.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius added: "Where dripping slander and skin-deep accusations gain no foothold, that ruler may be called clear-sighted."

sentences.zh: 」賢佞分別，官人有序，帥由舊章，敬重功勳，殊別嫡庶，如此則火得其性矣。

translations.literal: "When worthy and servile are distinguished, officers are ordered in sequence, commands follow the old statutes, merit is honored with weight, legitimate sons and concubine-born are clearly distinguished—thus fire obtains its nature.
translations.idiomatic: Distinguish true men from sycophants, order appointments by merit, hew to established statutes, honor service, and separate heir from concubine-born sons—then fire keeps its nature."

sentences.zh: 若乃通道不篤，或耀虛偽，讒夫昌，邪勝正，則火失其性矣。

translations.literal: But if the Way is not pursued earnestly, or empty show dazzles, slanderers flourish and the crooked overcome the straight—then fire loses its nature.
translations.idiomatic: Pursue the Way without conviction, parade hollow shows, let slanderers thrive and the crooked prevail—fire then loses its nature.

sentences.zh: 自上而降，及濫炎妄起，焚宗廟，燒宮館，雖興師眾，不能救也，是為火不炎上。

translations.literal: Then from above it descends: wanton flames arise of themselves, ancestral temples burn, palaces are consumed; though armies be raised in great numbers, they cannot save it—this is fire not blazing upward.
translations.idiomatic: Then flame drops from above—fires rage unchecked, torches the ancestral shrines and halls; no host however large can stop it: that is fire refusing to rise properly.

sentences.zh: 魏明帝五月，清商殿災。

translations.literal: In the fifth month of Wei Mingdi, the Qing Shang Hall burned.
translations.idiomatic: In the fifth month of Wei Emperor Ming, fire consumed the Qing Shang Hall.

sentences.zh: 初，帝為平原王，納河南虞氏為妃。

translations.literal: Earlier, when the emperor was Prince of Pingyuan he took the Yu clan of Henan as consort.
translations.idiomatic: Earlier, as Prince of Pingyuan, he had married a daughter of the Yu clan from Henan.

sentences.zh: 及即位，不以為-{后}-，更立典虞車工卒毛嘉女為-{后}-。

translations.literal: When he mounted the throne he did not make her empress; instead he raised the daughter of Mao Jia, chariot artisan conscript of the Arsenal Bureau, as empress.
translations.idiomatic: At his accession he refused her the empress's seat and raised instead the daughter of Mao Jia, a wheelwright in the palace workshops.

sentences.zh: -{后}-本仄微，非所宜升，以妾為妻之罰也。

translations.literal: The empress came from humble station—it was not fitting to elevate her; this was punishment for taking a concubine as wife.
translations.idiomatic: Her origins were low—she ought never to have been lifted so high; Heaven punished the offense of making a concubine into a wife.

sentences.zh: 六月，洛陽宮鞠室災。

translations.literal: In the sixth month the ball-court chamber of the Luoyang palace burned.
translations.idiomatic: That sixth month the polo grounds hall in the Luoyang palace burned.

sentences.zh: 二年四月，崇華殿災，延于南閣，繕復之。

translations.literal: In the fourth month of the second year Chonghua Hall burned, spreading to the southern wing; they repaired and restored it.
translations.idiomatic: The fourth month of the second year brought fire to Chonghua Hall, which spread to the south annex before crews rebuilt it.

sentences.zh: 至三年七月，此殿又災。

translations.literal: By the seventh month of the third year this hall burned again.
translations.idiomatic: By the seventh month of the third year the same hall burned again.

sentences.zh: 帝問高堂隆：「此何咎也？

translations.literal: The emperor asked Gao Tanglong: "What fault is this?
translations.idiomatic: The emperor asked Gao Tanglong, "What offense does this mark?

sentences.zh: 于禮寧有祈禳之義乎？

translations.literal: In ritual is there meaning in prayer and expiation?
translations.idiomatic: Does ritual allow us merely to pray it away?"

sentences.zh: 」對曰：「夫災變之發，皆所以明教誡也，惟率禮修德可以勝之。

translations.literal: "He answered: "When anomalies arise, they are all to clarify teaching and warning; only by leading with ritual and cultivating virtue can one overcome them.
translations.idiomatic: He replied, "Every prodigy is Heaven's lesson; only ritual observance and virtue can master it.

sentences.zh: 《易傳》曰：『上不儉，下不節，孽火燒其室。

translations.literal: The Yi Commentary says: 'If above is not frugal and below is not restrained, baleful fire burns his chamber.
translations.idiomatic: The Yi commentary warns: when those above will not stint and those below will not curb appetite, baleful fire consumes the hall.

sentences.zh: 』又曰：『君高其臺，天火為災。

translations.literal: 'It also says: 'If the lord raises his terrace high, Heaven's fire brings calamity.
translations.idiomatic: It adds: heap your terraces too high and Heaven's fire answers with disaster.

sentences.zh: 』此人君苟飾宮室，不知百姓空竭，故天應之以旱，火從高殿起也。

translations.literal: 'This is when the lord of men vainly adorns palace chambers and does not know the hundred clans are emptied and exhausted; therefore Heaven responds with drought, and fire rises from the high halls.'
translations.idiomatic: Heaven answers a ruler who decks out his halls while his people are bled dry: drought follows, and flame leaps from the highest roof.

sentences.zh: 案《舊占》曰：『災火之發，皆以臺榭宮室為誡。

translations.literal: According to the Old Omens: 'When calamity fire breaks out, it always takes terraces and palace chambers as its warning.'
translations.idiomatic: The Old Omens record: disaster fire always singles out towers and palace halls as its warning.

sentences.zh: 』今宜罷散作役，務從節約，清掃所災之處，不敢於此有所營造，萐莆嘉禾必生此地，以報陛下虔恭之德。

translations.literal: 'Now it is fitting to dismiss scattered labor projects, devote oneself to frugality, purify and sweep the burned sites, and not dare rebuild here—sweet-rush and fine grain will surely spring from this ground to repay Your Majesty's reverent virtue.'
translations.idiomatic: Cease the labor drafts, practice austerity, cleanse the scorched ground, and build nothing new there—auspicious grain will rise there to answer your sober virtue.

sentences.zh: 」帝不從。

translations.literal: The emperor did not comply.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor refused.

sentences.zh: 遂復崇華殿，改曰九龍。

translations.literal: Thereupon they rebuilt Chonghua Hall and renamed it Nine Dragons.
translations.idiomatic: They rebuilt Chonghua Hall and renamed it the Nine Dragons Hall.

sentences.zh: 以郡國前後言龍見者九，故以為名。

translations.literal: Because commanderies and kingdoms had successively reported nine dragon sightings, they used this as the name.
translations.idiomatic: Nine jurisdictions had reported dragon sightings; that number supplied the new name.

sentences.zh: 多棄法度，疲眾逞欲，以妾為妻之應也。

translations.literal: Many times casting aside standards, exhausting the masses and indulging desires—the response to taking a concubine as wife.
translations.idiomatic: It matched repeated disregard of law, grinding the people down for pleasure—the price of elevating a concubine to wife.

sentences.zh: 吳孫亮十二月，武昌端門災，改作，端門又災。

translations.literal: In the twelfth month under Sun Liang of Wu, Wuchang's main gate burned; they rebuilt, and the main gate burned again.
translations.idiomatic: In Sun Liang's twelfth month Wuchang's main gate caught fire; after repairs it burned again.

sentences.zh: 內殿門者，號令所出；

translations.literal: The inner hall gate is where commands issue forth;
translations.idiomatic: The inner hall gate is where edicts are proclaimed;

sentences.zh: 殿者，聽政之所。

translations.literal: the hall is where government is heard.
translations.idiomatic: the hall is where affairs of state are conducted.

sentences.zh: 是時諸葛恪執政，而矜慢放肆，孫峻總禁旅，而險害終著。

translations.literal: At this time Zhuge Ke held power and was arrogant, reckless, and wanton; Sun Jun commanded the palace guard and in the end his vicious harm stood revealed.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Ke governed with swagger and license; Sun Jun led the palace troops—cruel harm showed itself in the end.

sentences.zh: 武昌，孫氏尊號所始。

translations.literal: Wuchang was where the Sun house first took its royal title.
translations.idiomatic: Wuchang was where the Sun clan first assumed kingship.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，宜除其貴要之首者，恪果喪眾殄人，峻授政於綝，綝廢亮也。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say one ought to remove the chief of those honored and powerful—Ke indeed lost his host and was destroyed; Jun handed power to Lin, who deposed Liang.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven seemed to demand the head of the mighty: Ke lost his army and his life, Jun passed power to Sun Lin, and Lin cast Sun Liang down.

sentences.zh: 或曰，孫權毀撤武昌以增太初宮，諸葛恪有遷都意，更起門殿，事非時宜，故見災也。

translations.literal: Some say Sun Quan demolished Wuchang to enlarge the Taichu Palace; Zhuge Ke intended to move the capital and rebuilt gate and hall—untimely business—hence the anomaly appeared.
translations.idiomatic: Others blame Sun Quan's dismantling of Wuchang for Taichu Palace and Zhuge Ke's plan to move the capital and rebuild gates—ill-timed work that drew the portent.

sentences.zh: 京房《易傳》曰：「君不思道，厥妖火燒宮。」

translations.literal: Jing Fang's Yi Commentary says: "If the lord does not ponder the Way, its prodigy is fire burning the palace."
translations.idiomatic: Jing Fang's Yi commentary: neglect the Way and the omen is flame consuming the palace.

sentences.zh: 二月朔，建鄴火，人之火也。

translations.literal: On the new moon of the second month Jianye burned—human-kindled fire.
translations.idiomatic: Jianye burned on the second month's new moon—fire set by human hands.

sentences.zh: 是秋，孫綝始執政，矯以亮詔殺呂據、滕胤。

translations.literal: That autumn Sun Lin first seized government and forged Liang's edict to kill Lu Ju and Teng Yin.
translations.idiomatic: That autumn Sun Lin took power and forged an edict in Sun Liang's name to execute Lu Ju and Teng Yin.

sentences.zh: 明年，又輒殺硃異。

translations.literal: The next year he again executed Zhu Yi without authority.
translations.idiomatic: The next year he put Zhu Yi to death on his own authority.

sentences.zh: 棄法律逐功臣之罰也。

translations.literal: Punishment for casting aside law and driving away meritorious ministers.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven's sentence for abandoning statute and banishing loyal servants.

sentences.zh: 孫休二月，城西門北樓災。

translations.literal: In the second month under Sun Xiu, the north tower of the west gate burned.
translations.idiomatic: Under Sun Xiu, in the second month, the north tower at the west gate burned.

sentences.zh: 六年十月，石頭小城火，燒西南百八十丈。

translations.literal: In the tenth month of the sixth year Shitou minor fort burned—one hundred eighty zhang of the southwest caught fire.
translations.idiomatic: In the sixth year's tenth month fire swept the Shitou citadel, scorching a hundred eighty zhang along the southwest wall.

sentences.zh: 是時嬖人張布專擅國勢，多行無禮，而韋昭、盛沖終斥不用，兼遣察戰等為內史，驚擾州郡，致使交趾反亂，是其咎也。

translations.literal: At this time favorite Zhang Bu monopolized state power and acted lawlessly in many ways, while Wei Zhao and Sheng Chong were rejected to the end and not employed; moreover he sent battle inspectors and others as interior clerks, alarming commanderies and prefectures until Jiaozhi rebelled—the fault lay here.
translations.idiomatic: Favorite Zhang Bu dominated the court and flouted propriety; Wei Zhao and Sheng Chong remained sidelined; inspection officers installed as interior clerks harassed the provinces until Jiaozhi rose in revolt—that was the guilt.

sentences.zh: 孫皓三月，大火，燒萬餘家，死者七百人。

translations.literal: In the third month under Sun Hao a great fire burned over ten thousand households; seven hundred died.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao's third month brought a conflagration—ten thousand homes lost, seven hundred lives.

sentences.zh: 案《春秋》齊大災，劉向以為桓公好內，聽女口，妻妾數更之罰也。

translations.literal: According to the Spring and Autumn great fire in Qi—Liu Xiang took it that Duke Huan favored the inner quarters, listened to women's words, and repeatedly changed wives—the punishment.
translations.idiomatic: The Spring and Autumn records Qi's great blaze; Liu Xiang blamed Duke Huan's harem intrigues and shifting wives.

sentences.zh: 時皓制令詭暴，蕩棄法度，勞臣名士，誅斥甚眾，後宮萬餘，女謁數行，其中隆寵佩皇后璽綬者又多矣，故有大火。

translations.literal: At that time Hao's orders were cruel and violent, law was abandoned, worthy ministers and noted scholars were executed or banished in great numbers; the rear palace held over ten thousand women and women's petitions ran unchecked; among them many won lavish favor and wore the empress's seal and ribbon—hence the great fire.
translations.idiomatic: Hao ruled by cruelty and caprice, cast law aside, purged scholars and officials, kept ten thousand palace women, and let favorites—even some bearing empress regalia—run wild; the inferno answered that.

sentences.zh: 武帝三月乙丑，震災西閣楚王所止坊及臨商觀窗。

translations.literal: On yichou day in the third month of Wudi, lightning struck the Prince of Chu's compound by the west pavilion and the windows of the Linshang Observatory.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu's third month, yichou day: lightning scarred the Prince of Chu's west-pavilion ward and the Linshang Observatory windows.

sentences.zh: 十年四月癸丑，崇賢殿災。

translations.literal: On guichou day in the fourth month of the tenth year Chongxian Hall burned.
translations.idiomatic: The tenth year's fourth month, guichou day: Chongxian Hall burned.

sentences.zh: 十一月庚辰，含章鞠室、修成堂前廡、景坊東屋、暉章殿南閣火。

translations.literal: On gengchen day in the eleventh month Hanzhang ball court, the gallery before Xiucheng Hall, the east wing of Jingfang, and the south wing of Huizhang Hall caught fire.
translations.idiomatic: Eleventh month, gengchen day: fire took Hanzhang racquet hall, Xiucheng Hall's front colonnade, Jingfang's east wing, and Huizhang Hall's south arcade.

sentences.zh: 時有上書曰：「漢王氏五侯，兄弟迭任，今楊氏三公，並在大位，故天變屢見，竊為陛下憂之。

translations.literal: At this time a memorial came up saying: "In Han the Wang nobles in five enfeoffments, brothers taking turns in office; now the Yang three dukes all hold high rank—therefore Heaven's changes appear repeatedly; I privately worry for Your Majesty."
translations.idiomatic: A memorial warned: Han's five Wang marquises rotated power among brothers; now three Yang dukes tower together—Heaven keeps signaling alarm.

sentences.zh: 」由是楊珧求退。

translations.literal: On this account Yang Yao asked to retire.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Yao thereupon sought to withdraw.

sentences.zh: 是時帝納馮紞之間，廢張華之功，聽楊駿之讒，離衛瓘之寵，此逐功臣之罰也。

translations.literal: At this time the emperor accepted Feng Xian's slander, voided Zhang Hua's achievements, listened to Yang Jun's defamation, and parted from Wei Guan's favor—punishment for driving away meritorious ministers.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor heeded Feng Xian's slander, dismissed Zhang Hua's service, swallowed Yang Jun's malice, and cast off Wei Guan—Heaven's rebuke for banishing loyal ministers.

sentences.zh: 明年，宮車宴駕。

translations.literal: The next year the imperial carriage halted forever.
translations.idiomatic: The next year the emperor died.

sentences.zh: 其後楚王承竊發之旨，戮害二公，身亦不免。

translations.literal: Afterward the Prince of Chu acted on a prompt to secret rebellion, slaughtered the two dukes, and himself did not escape.
translations.idiomatic: Then the Prince of Chu, seizing a secret pretext, slew both dukes and soon perished himself.

sentences.zh: 震災其坊，又天意乎。

translations.literal: Lightning struck his compound—was it again Heaven's intent?
translations.idiomatic: Lightning had scarred his ward—Heaven speaking again?

sentences.zh: 惠帝閏月庚寅，武庫火。

translations.literal: On gengyin day in the intercalary month under Huidi, the armory burned.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Hui, intercalary month, gengyin day: the imperial armory burned.

sentences.zh: 張華疑有亂，先命固守，然後救火。

translations.literal: Zhang Hua suspected trouble and first ordered a tight guard, then fought the fire.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Hua feared revolt, secured the site first, then fought the flames.

sentences.zh: 是以累代異寶，王莽頭，孔子屐，漢高祖斷白蛇劍及二百八萬器械，一時蕩盡。

translations.literal: Therefore treasures amassed through generations—Wang Mang's head, Confucius's sandal, Han Gaozu's sword that split the white snake, and 2.08 million weapons—were in one moment utterly consumed.
translations.idiomatic: Generations of relics vanished at once: Wang Mang's skull, Confucius's sandal, Gaozu's sword from the white-snake omen, and 2.08 million weapons.

sentences.zh: 是後湣懷太子見殺之罰也。

translations.literal: This was punishment for the heir apparent Minhuai being killed.
translations.idiomatic: It foretold the murder of Crown Prince Minhuai.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，夫設險擊柝，所以固其國，儲積戒器，所以戒不虞。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: palisades and night-watch drums exist to secure the state; stored arms exist to guard against the unforeseen.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven warned: ramparts and night watches brace the realm; arsenals guard against surprise.

sentences.zh: 今塚嗣將傾，社稷將泯，禁兵無所復施，皇旅又將誰衛。

translations.literal: Now the heir will soon fall, the altars of soil and grain will perish, palace troops have nowhere to be deployed again—who then will guard the royal host?
translations.idiomatic: The heir teeters, the altars face ruin, palace guards lose purpose—who will shield the throne?

sentences.zh: 帝后不悟，終喪四海，是其應也。

translations.literal: Emperor and empress did not wake to it and in the end lost the realm within the four seas—this was its response.
translations.idiomatic: Ruler and consort ignored it and lost the empire—that was the fulfillment.

sentences.zh: 張華、閻纂皆曰，武庫火而氐羌反，太子見廢，則四海可知。」

translations.literal: Zhang Hua and Yan Zuan both said: "When the armory burns while the Di and Qiang revolt and the heir apparent is deposed, the meaning for all within the seas may be known."
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Hua and Yan Zuan said: armory fire with Di and Qiang in revolt and the heir deposed tells you all you need of the realm.

sentences.zh: 八年十一月，高原陵火。

translations.literal: In the eleventh month of the eighth year Gaoyuan Mausoleum burned.
translations.idiomatic: Eighth year, eleventh month: Gaoyuan Mausoleum burned.

sentences.zh: 是時賈后凶恣，賈謐擅朝，惡積罪稔，宜見誅絕。

translations.literal: At this time Empress Jia was fierce and unbridled, Jia Mi monopolized court, evil accumulated and guilt ripened—she ought to have been executed and cut off.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Jia raged unchecked, Jia Mi dominated court—guilt had ripened; both deserved execution.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，臣妾之不可者，雖親貴莫比，猶宜忍而誅之，如吾燔高原陵也。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: what cannot be tolerated in concubines and ministers—even if kin and noble—should still be endured and executed, as I burn Gaoyuan Mausoleum.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven said: intolerable servants and consorts, however royal, must be cut down—as I scorch Gaoyuan Mausoleum.

sentences.zh: 帝既眊弱，而張華又不納裴頠、劉卞之謀，故後遂與謐殺太子也。

translations.literal: The emperor was already dim and weak, and Zhang Hua again did not adopt Pei Wei's and Liu Bian's plans—hence afterward she joined Mi in killing the heir.
translations.idiomatic: The feckless emperor spurned Pei Wei and Liu Bian's counsel; the empress and Jia Mi went on to kill the heir.

sentences.zh: 干寶以為「高原陵火，太子廢之應。

translations.literal: Gan Bao took it that "Gaoyuan Mausoleum burning was the response to the heir apparent's deposition."
translations.idiomatic: Gan Bao read Gaoyuan's blaze as an answer to the crown prince's deposition.

sentences.zh: 漢武帝世，高園便殿火，董仲舒對與此占同」。

translations.literal: In Emperor Wu of Han's reign the side hall of Gao Park burned; Dong Zhongshu's response matched this omen."
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu of Han saw Gao Park's hall burn; Dong Zhongshu's reading matched this sign."

sentences.zh: ，帝納皇后羊氏，-{后}-將入宮，衣中忽有火，眾咸怪之。

translations.literal: , the emperor took Empress Yang; when the empress was about to enter the palace, fire suddenly appeared in her clothing and all marveled.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor took Empress Yang; as she entered the palace, flame flickered in her robes—a wonder to all.

sentences.zh: ，成都王遂廢-{后}-，處之金墉城。

translations.literal: , the Prince of Chengdu then deposed the empress and confined her to Jinyong City.
translations.idiomatic: The Prince of Chengdu deposed her and immured her in Jinyong fortress.

sentences.zh: 是後還立，立而復廢者四。

translations.literal: Afterward she was restored, then deposed four times after installation.
translations.idiomatic: She was restored and cast down four times thereafter.

sentences.zh: 又詔賜死，荀籓表全之。

translations.literal: Again an edict ordered her to die; Xun Fan memorialized to spare her.
translations.idiomatic: Another death edict came; Xun Fan pleaded for her life.

sentences.zh: 雖來還在位，然憂逼折辱，終古未聞。

translations.literal: Though she returned and held position, yet anxiety, coercion, and humiliation—never heard of through the ages.
translations.idiomatic: Though she sometimes returned to rank, the fear and humiliation were without precedent.

sentences.zh: 此孽火之應也。

translations.literal: This was the response of baleful fire.
translations.idiomatic: Baleful fire had spoken.

sentences.zh: 七月甲午，尚書諸曹火起，延崇禮闥及閣道。

translations.literal: On jiawu day in the seventh month fire broke out in the various bureaus of the Secretariat, spreading to Chongli Gate and the covered walkway.
translations.idiomatic: Seventh month, jiawu day: Secretariat bureaus ignited; flames spread to Chongli Gate and the cloister.

sentences.zh: 夫百揆王化之本，王者棄法津之應也。

translations.literal: The hundred offices are root of royal transformation—response to the king casting aside law.
translations.idiomatic: The hundred offices anchor royal transformation—Heaven answered a ruler who abandoned law.

sentences.zh: 後清河王覃入嗣，不終於位，又殺太子之罰也。

translations.literal: Later Prince Qinghe Tan entered as heir but did not finish his tenure—again punishment for killing the heir apparent.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Qinghe Tan succeeded but never finished his mandate—another reckoning for killing an heir.

sentences.zh: 孝懷帝十一月，襄陽火，燒死者三千餘人。

translations.literal: In the eleventh month under Emperor Huai, Xiangyang burned—three thousand and more burned to death.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Huai's eleventh month: Xiangyang burned; three thousand perished in the flames.

sentences.zh: 是時王如自號大將軍、司雍二州牧，眾四五萬，攻略郡縣。

translations.literal: At this time Wang Ru styled himself grand general and shepherd of Si and Yong with forty or fifty thousand followers raiding commanderies and counties.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Ru styled himself grand general and governor of Si and Yong, forty or fifty thousand strong, pillaging towns.

sentences.zh: 此下陵上，陽失其節之應也。

translations.literal: This was the response to inferiors pressing superiors and yang losing its measure.
translations.idiomatic: Inferiors lording over superiors—yang had lost its pitch.

sentences.zh: 元帝太興中，王敦鎮武昌，武昌災，火起，興眾救之，救於此而發於彼，東西南北數十處俱應，數日不絕。

translations.literal: In Taixing under Yuandi Wang Dun held Wuchang; Wuchang suffered disaster—fire broke out; they raised crowds to fight it but wherever they fought it elsewhere—several tens of places east west south north all blazed at once for several days without cease.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Yuan, Wang Dun at Wuchang faced fire that jumped from spot to spot—dozens of outbreaks across the compass burned for days.

sentences.zh: 舊說所謂「濫炎妄起，雖興師眾，不能救之」之謂也。

translations.literal: The old gloss calls this "wantonly flames arise of themselves—though hosts be raised they cannot save them."
translations.idiomatic: Ancient gloss: wildfire everywhere—no army can stamp it out.

sentences.zh: 干寶以為「此臣而君行，亢陽失節，是為王敦陵上，有無君之心，故災也。」

translations.literal: Gan Bao took it that "This is minister comporting as lord; excessive yang loses its measure—this is Wang Dun lording over superiors with a heart that knows no lord—hence disaster."
translations.idiomatic: Gan Bao called it ministers acting as rulers—yang run wild—Wang Dun bullying his sovereign, a heart without liege.

sentences.zh: 正月癸巳，京師大火。

translations.literal: On guisi day in the first month the capital burned greatly.
translations.idiomatic: First month, guisi day: great fire in the capital.

sentences.zh: 三月，饒安、東光、安陵三縣火，燒七千餘家，死者萬五千人。

translations.literal: In the third month Rao'an, Dongguang, and Anling three counties burned—seven thousand and more households, fifteen thousand dead.
translations.idiomatic: Third month: Rao'an, Dongguang, and Anling burned—seven thousand homes, fifteen thousand dead.

sentences.zh: 明帝正月，京都火。

translations.literal: In the first month under Mingdi the capital burned.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ming's first month: the capital burned.

sentences.zh: 是時王敦威侮朝廷，多行無禮，內外臣下咸懷怨毒，極陰生陽也。

translations.literal: At this time Wang Dun insulted and threatened court, acted lawlessly in many ways; officials within and without all harbored resentment and poison—extreme yin begetting yang.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun insulted the court and broke protocol; resentment seethed inside and out—extreme yin birthing yang.

sentences.zh: 成帝五月，京師火。

translations.literal: In the fifth month under Chengdi the capital burned.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Cheng's fifth month: capital fire.

sentences.zh: 康帝七月庚申，吳郡災。

translations.literal: On gengshen day in the seventh month under Kangdi Wu commandery suffered disaster.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Kang, seventh month, gengshen day: Wu commandery disaster.

sentences.zh: 穆帝六月，震災石季龍太武殿及兩廟端門。

translations.literal: In the sixth month under Mudi lightning struck Shi Hu's Taiwu Hall and the main gates of the two temples.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Mu's sixth month: lightning shattered Shi Hu's Taiwu Hall and the twin temples' main gates.

sentences.zh: 震災月餘乃滅，金石皆盡。

translations.literal: The lightning disaster over a month before it died out—metal and stone were all gone.
translations.idiomatic: The lightning lasted over a month; metal and stone melted away.

sentences.zh: 其後季龍死，大亂，遂滅亡。

translations.literal: Afterward Ji Hu died, great chaos followed, and they perished.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Hu died, chaos followed, and Zhao fell.

sentences.zh: 海西公太和中，郗愔為會稽太守。

translations.literal: Under Duke of Haixi in Taihe years Xi Yin was Kuaiji prefect.
translations.idiomatic: Under Duke Haixi, during Taihe, Xi Yin governed Kuaiji.

sentences.zh: 六月大旱災，火燒數千家。

translations.literal: In the sixth month great drought disaster—fire burned several thousand households.
translations.idiomatic: Sixth month drought and fire claimed thousands of homes.

sentences.zh: 延及山陰倉米數百萬斛，炎煙蔽天，不可撲滅。

translations.literal: It spread to Shanyin granary—several million hu of rice—flame and smoke veiled the sky and could not be beaten out.
translations.idiomatic: Flames reached Shanyin's granaries—millions of hu—smoke veiling the sky, unstoppable.

sentences.zh: 此亦桓溫強盛，將廢海西，極陰生陽之應也。

translations.literal: This too was Huan Wen's might waxing to depose Duke of Haixi—extreme yin begetting yang.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen's power was poised to depose Duke Haixi—again extreme yin flashing into yang.

sentences.zh: 孝武帝三月，京師風火大起。

translations.literal: In the third month under Xiaowudi great wind fire arose in the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowu's third month: wind-driven fire raged in the capital.

sentences.zh: 是時桓溫入朝，志在陵上，少主踐位，人懷憂恐，此與太寧火事同。

translations.literal: At this time Huan Wen entered court intending to overbear superiors; the young lord had just taken the throne and men harbored fear—same as the Taining fire affair.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen entered court bent on dominating the young emperor—fear everywhere, as in the Taining fires.

sentences.zh: 正月，國子學生因風放火，焚房百餘間。

translations.literal: In the first month students of the Imperial Academy used wind to set fire and burned over a hundred rooms.
translations.idiomatic: First month: Imperial Academy students used the wind to torch more than a hundred rooms.

sentences.zh: 是後考課不厲，賞黜無章。

translations.literal: Afterward examinations were not strict, rewards and dismissals lacked rule.
translations.idiomatic: Afterward examinations slackened; rewards and dismissals followed no rule.

sentences.zh: 蓋有育才之名，而無收賢之實，此不哲之罰先兆也。

translations.literal: They had the name of nurturing talent but not the reality of gathering worthies—first omen of punishment for lack of wisdom.
translations.idiomatic: The court cultivated talent in name but not in fact—an early sign of unwisdom's price.

sentences.zh: 十三年十二月乙未，延賢堂災。

translations.literal: On yiwei day in the twelfth month of the thirteenth year Yanxian Hall burned.
translations.idiomatic: Thirteenth year, twelfth month, yiwei day: Yanxian Hall burned.

sentences.zh: 是月丙申，螽斯則百堂及客館、驃騎府庫皆災。

translations.literal: That month on bingshen Zhongsi Ze Bai Hall, guest lodges, and the mounted escort armory all burned.
translations.idiomatic: Same month, bingshen day: Zhongsi Ze Bai Hall, guest quarters, and the cavalry command depot burned.

sentences.zh: 于時朝多弊政，衰陵日兆，不哲之罰，皆有象類。

translations.literal: At that time court held many bad policies, decline and ruin showed daily—punishments for unwisdom all had images and kinds.
translations.idiomatic: Court policy rotted and decline showed daily—every unwisdom left its token.

sentences.zh: 主相不悟，終至亂亡。

translations.literal: Ruler and chief minister did not awaken and in the end fell to chaos and ruin.
translations.idiomatic: Prince and minister slept on until ruin.

sentences.zh: 會稽王道子寵倖尼及姏母，各樹用其親戚，乃至出入宮掖，禮見人主。

translations.literal: Prince of Kuaiji Daozi favored nuns and wet-nurses, each installing kin to office until they passed in and out of the palace and met the sovereign by ritual.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Daozi of Kuaiji favored nuns and nurses, packing offices with kin who traversed the palace as if equals.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，登延賢堂及客館者多非其人，故災之也。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: many who ascended Yanxian Hall and guest lodges were not fit men—therefore it burned them.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven warned: unworthy men filled Yanxian Hall and the guest lodges—so flame purged them.

sentences.zh: 又，孝武帝更不立皇后，寵倖微賤張夫人，夫人驕妒，皇子不繁，乖「螽斯則百」之道，故災其殿焉。

translations.literal: Moreover Xiaowudi never again established an empress but favored lowborn Lady Zhang—proud and jealous—sons of the dragon were not numerous, contradicting the way of "locusts grant a hundred"—therefore that hall burned.
translations.idiomatic: Xiaowudi kept no empress but showered lowborn Lady Zhang—jealous and proud—so heirs were few, mocking the ode's prayer for many sons—the hall answered.

sentences.zh: 道子復賞賜不節，故府庫被災，斯亦其罰也。

translations.literal: Daozi again gave rewards without measure—hence the treasury burned—this too was its punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Daozi spent the treasury without measure—fire took the stores as payment.

sentences.zh: 安帝三月，龍舟二乘災，是水沴火也。

translations.literal: In the third month under Andi two dragon boats burned—water encroaching on fire.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor An's third month: two dragon barges burned—water's revenge on fire.

sentences.zh: 其後桓玄篡位，帝乃播越。

translations.literal: Afterward Huan Xuan usurped and the emperor was driven to wander.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan seized the throne and the emperor fled.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，王者流遷，不復禦龍舟，故災之耳。

translations.literal: Heaven's warning seemed to say: the king drifts in exile and no longer rides dragon boats—therefore it burned them.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven said the wanderer-king would steer no dragon barges—so they burned.

sentences.zh: 八月庚子，尚書下舍曹火。

translations.literal: On gengzi day in the eighth month the lower Secretariat barracks burned.
translations.idiomatic: Eighth month, gengzi day: the lower Secretariat barracks burned.

sentences.zh: 時桓玄遙錄尚書，故天火，示不復居也。

translations.literal: At this time Huan Xuan held the Secretariat at a distance—therefore Heaven's fire showed he would not dwell there again.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan held the Secretariat by proxy—Heaven's fire said he would not stay.

sentences.zh: 三年，盧循攻略廣州，刺史吳隱之閉城固守。

translations.literal: In the third year Lu Xun attacked Guangzhou; Inspector Wu Yinzi shut the city fast.
translations.idiomatic: Third year: Lu Xun besieged Guangzhou; Inspector Wu Yinzi held the walls.

sentences.zh: 其十月壬戌夜，火起。

translations.literal: That tenth month on renxu night fire broke out.
translations.idiomatic: Tenth month, renxu night: fire broke out.

sentences.zh: 時百姓避寇盈滿城內，隱之懼有應賊者，但務嚴兵，不先救火。

translations.literal: At the time refugees fleeing bandits filled the city; Yinzi feared collaborators inside and only pressed strict guards, not fighting fire first.
translations.idiomatic: Refugees packed the town; Yinzi feared traitors and manned the walls instead of fighting the blaze.

sentences.zh: 由是府舍焚蕩，燒死者萬餘人，因遂散潰，悉為賊擒。

translations.literal: Thereupon government buildings burned out; over ten thousand burned to death; they scattered and were routed and all were seized by bandits.
translations.idiomatic: Administration halls burned; ten thousand died; the defense collapsed and rebels took everyone.

sentences.zh: 七月丁酉，尚書殿中吏部曹火。

translations.literal: On dingyou day in the seventh month the Palace Secretariat Personnel Bureau burned.
translations.idiomatic: Seventh month, dingyou day: the Secretariat's personnel bureau burned.

sentences.zh: 九年，京都大火，燒數千家。

translations.literal: In the ninth year the capital had great fire—several thousand households burned.
translations.idiomatic: Ninth year: capital inferno—thousands of homes lost.

sentences.zh: 十一年，京都所在大行火災，吳界尤甚。

translations.literal: In the eleventh year fires ran rampant wherever the capital stood; east of the Yangzi was worst.
translations.idiomatic: The eleventh year saw fires rage across the capital region and even fiercer in Wu.

sentences.zh: 火防甚峻，猶自不絕。

translations.literal: Fire precautions were extremely strict, yet they still did not cease.
translations.idiomatic: Precautions ran severe; still the blazes would not stop.

sentences.zh: 王弘時為吳郡，晝在聽事，見天上有一赤物下，狀如信幡，遙集路南人家屋上，火即大發。

translations.literal: Wang Hong was then prefect of Wu; in daylight in the audience hall he saw a red object descend from the sky, shaped like a signal banner, alight from afar on a house roof south of the road—fire immediately broke out great.
translations.idiomatic: Prefect Wang Hong, in session by day, watched a red thing fall like a banner and settle on a roof; flame burst forth at once.

sentences.zh: 弘知天為之災，故不罪火主。

translations.literal: Hong knew Heaven had made this disaster, therefore he did not punish the fire’s human source.
translations.idiomatic: He read it as Heaven’s work and blamed no householder.

sentences.zh: 此帝室衰微之應也。

translations.literal: This was the response to the imperial house’s decline.
translations.idiomatic: The omen matched a fading house of Sima.

translations.literal: Equals sign used as a typographical section divider.
translations.idiomatic: Typographical section divider.

sentences.zh: 土

translations.literal: Earth.
translations.idiomatic: Earth.

sentences.zh: =《傳》曰：「修宮室，飾臺榭，內淫亂，犯親戚，侮兄弟，則稼穡不成。」

translations.literal: =The Tradition says: “If one builds palace chambers, adorns terraces and pavilions, debauches within the inner quarters, offends kin, and insults brothers—then sowing and reaping do not succeed.”
translations.idiomatic: The gloss: palace-building, terrace ornament, inner debauchery, kin violated, brothers mocked—then the harvest fails.

sentences.zh: 說曰：土，中央，生萬物者也。

translations.literal: The explanation says: Earth is the center; it gives birth to the myriad things.
translations.idiomatic: Earth sits at the center and brings forth all things.

sentences.zh: 其于王者，為內事，宮室、夫婦、親屬，亦相生者也。

translations.literal: As for the kingly person, it governs inner affairs—palace chambers, husband and wife, kin—they likewise generate one another.
translations.idiomatic: For the throne it means the inner realm: halls, marriage, kin—all mutually sustaining.

sentences.zh: 古者天子諸侯，宮廟大小高卑有制，-{后}-夫人媵妾多少有度，九族親疏長幼有序。

translations.literal: In antiquity Son of Heaven and feudal lords had regulated size and height of palace temples; empress, consorts, and concubines had measured numbers; the nine kindreds had ordered distance and seniority.
translations.idiomatic: Ancient rulers fixed temple scale, numbered wives and concubines, and ranked the nine agnates.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「禮，與其奢也，寧儉。

translations.literal: Confucius said: “In ritual, rather than extravagance, better frugality.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said: in ritual prefer thrift to waste.

sentences.zh: 」故禹卑宮室，文王刑于寡妻，此聖人之所以昭教化也。

translations.literal: ”Therefore Yu kept palace chambers low; King Wen set example for his lone wife—this is how sages displayed transformation through teaching.
translations.idiomatic: Hence Yu’s humble halls and King Wen’s model for his wife—how sages taught the realm.

sentences.zh: 如此，則土得其性矣。

translations.literal: Thus earth obtains its nature.
translations.idiomatic: Then earth keeps its true nature.

sentences.zh: 若乃奢淫驕慢，則土失其性。

translations.literal: But if there is extravagance, debauchery, arrogance, and sloth—then earth loses its nature.
translations.idiomatic: Extravagance, lust, pride, and sloth strip earth of its nature.

sentences.zh: 亡水旱之災而草木百穀不熟，是為稼穡不成。

translations.literal: Though there be no flood or drought disaster, yet grasses, trees, and the hundred grains do not ripen—this is called sowing and reaping not succeeding.
translations.idiomatic: Without flood or drought, crops still refuse to ripen—that is failure of harvest.

sentences.zh: 吳孫皓時，常歲無水旱，苗稼豐美而實不成，百姓以饑，闔境皆然，連歲不已。

translations.literal: Under Sun Hao of Wu, ordinary years had neither flood nor drought; seedlings flourished beautifully yet grain did not fill; the hundred clans starved—the whole territory was thus, year after year without end.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao’s reign saw fair weather and lush stands that bore no grain—famine everywhere, year on year.

sentences.zh: 吳人以為傷露，非也。

translations.literal: Wu people took it as harm from dew—this is not so.
translations.idiomatic: Wu blamed dew damage—wrongly.

sentences.zh: 案劉向《春秋說》曰「水旱當書，不書水旱而曰大無麥禾者，土氣不養，稼穡不成」，此其義也。

translations.literal: According to Liu Xiang’s Spring and Autumn Explanation: “Flood and drought ought to be recorded; when flood and drought are not recorded but it says great lack of wheat and grain—earth’s qi does not nourish; sowing and reaping do not succeed”—this is its meaning.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xiang read the Annals: omitting flood or drought yet recording total crop failure means earth failed to nurture.

sentences.zh: 皓初遷都武昌，尋還建鄴，又起新館，綴飾珠玉，壯麗過甚，破壞諸營，增廣苑囿，犯暑妨農，官私疲怠。

translations.literal: Hao first moved the capital to Wuchang, soon returned to Jianye, again raised new lodges, studded them with pearl and jade, surpassing splendor, demolished various camps, enlarged parks and preserves, violated the hot season and harmed farming—official and private alike exhausted and slack.
translations.idiomatic: Hao shifted to Wuchang, came back to Jianye, threw up jeweled halls beyond measure, tore down camps for gardens, worked through summer heat—state and people wore out.

sentences.zh: 《月令》，季夏不可以興土功，

translations.literal: The Monthly Ordinance: in the last month of summer one must not raise earth works,
translations.idiomatic: The Monthly Ordinance forbids earthworks in late summer—

sentences.zh: 皓皆冒之。

translations.literal: Hao transgressed them all.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao broke every rule.

sentences.zh: 此修宮室飾臺榭之罰也。

translations.literal: This was punishment for building palace chambers and adorning terraces and pavilions.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s sentence for palace-building and terrace finery.

sentences.zh: 元帝，吳郡、吳興、東陽無麥禾，大饑。

translations.literal: Under Yuandi Wu commandery, Wuxing, and Dongyang had no wheat or grain—great famine.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan’s reign: Wu, Wuxing, and Dongyang lost their crops—great famine.

sentences.zh: 成帝，無麥禾，天下大饑。

translations.literal: Under Chengdi there was no wheat or grain—great famine in the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Cheng: empire-wide crop failure and famine.

sentences.zh: 穆帝，三麥不登。

translations.literal: Under Mudi the three wheats did not ripen.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Mu: three seasons of wheat failed.

sentences.zh: 十二年，大無麥。

translations.literal: In the twelfth year great lack of wheat.
translations.idiomatic: Twelfth year: almost no wheat.

sentences.zh: 孝武，無麥禾，天下大饑。

translations.literal: Under Xiaowudi no wheat or grain—great famine in the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowu: again no grain empire-wide.

sentences.zh: 安帝，無麥禾，天下大饑。

translations.literal: Under Andi no wheat or grain—great famine in the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor An: the same dearth across the land.

translations.literal: Equals sign used as a typographical section divider.
translations.idiomatic: Typographical section divider.

sentences.zh: 金

translations.literal: Metal.
translations.idiomatic: Metal.

sentences.zh: =《傳》曰：「好戰攻，輕百姓，飾城郭，侵邊境，則金不從革。」

translations.literal: =The Tradition says: “If one loves campaigning and attack, esteems the hundred clans lightly, adorns walls and moats, and encroaches on borderlands—then metal does not yield to the forge.”
translations.idiomatic: Love war, despise the people, gild your walls, raid the frontiers—metal then refuses the smith.

sentences.zh: 說曰：金，西方，萬物既成，殺氣之始也。

translations.literal: The explanation says: Metal is the west; the myriad things having matured, it is the beginning of killing qi.
translations.idiomatic: Metal is west—the season when growth ends and killing qi begins.

sentences.zh: 故立秋而鷹隼擊，秋分而微霜降。

translations.literal: Therefore at Beginning of Autumn hawks and falcons strike; at Autumn Equinox slight frost descends.
translations.idiomatic: Autumn’s start brings raptors; equinox brings first frost.

sentences.zh: 其于王事，出軍行師，把旄杖鉞，誓士眾，抗威武，所以征叛逆，止暴亂也。

translations.literal: As for affairs of kingship: raising armies, marching hosts, grasping yak-tail banners and wielding axes, swearing the ranks, displaying martial awe—these serve to punish rebellion and stop violence.
translations.idiomatic: Kings wage war with banners and axes to crush rebels and quell chaos.

sentences.zh: 《詩》云：「有虔執鉞，如火烈烈。

translations.literal: The Odes says: “Reverent they grasp the axes, blazing like fire.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Odes: axes raised in awful splendor, fierce as flame.

sentences.zh: 」又曰：「載戢干戈，載橐弓矢。

translations.literal: ”It also says: “Then stash shields and spears, then bag bows and arrows.
translations.idiomatic: It also says: put away arms and bundle the bows.

sentences.zh: 」動靜應宜，說以犯難，人忘其死，金得其性矣。

translations.literal: ”Movement and stillness answer what is fitting; persuasion through braving hardship—men forget their death—metal obtains its nature.
translations.idiomatic: When war and peace fit the hour and men face peril willingly, metal keeps its nature.

sentences.zh: 若乃貪欲恣睢，務立威勝，不重人命，則金失其性。

translations.literal: But if greed and desire run riot, effort goes to establishing awe and victory, and human lives are not valued—then metal loses its nature.
translations.idiomatic: Greed for glory, thirst for terror, contempt for life—metal loses its nature.

sentences.zh: 蓋工冶鑄金鐵，冰滯涸堅，不成者眾，乃為變怪，是為金不從革。

translations.literal: Thus craftsmen smelt gold and iron—ice stuck, dried hard—many fail to form; then come prodigies—this is metal not yielding to change.
translations.idiomatic: Foundries seize up; castings fail—strange omens of metal refusing the forge.

sentences.zh: 魏時張掖石瑞，雖是晉之符命，而于魏為妖。

translations.literal: In Wei times the Zhangye stone omen, though it was Jin’s mandate token, for Wei was an anomaly.
translations.idiomatic: Wei’s Zhangye stone foretold Jin yet spelled Wei’s ill omen.

sentences.zh: 好攻戰，輕百姓，飾城郭，侵邊境，魏氏三祖皆有其事。

translations.literal: Loving attack warfare, esteeming the hundred clans lightly, adorning walls and moats, encroaching on borderlands—the three Wei ancestors all had these deeds.
translations.idiomatic: Wei’s three founding rulers loved war, neglected the people, dressed their walls, and raided borders.

sentences.zh: 石圖發于非常之文，此不從革之異也。

translations.literal: The stone chart issued from extraordinary script—this is the anomaly of not yielding to change.
translations.idiomatic: Strange characters on stone chart metal’s refusal to temper.

sentences.zh: 晉定大業，多斃曹氏，石瑞文「大討曹」之應也。

translations.literal: Jin settled the great enterprise and largely destroyed the Cao house—the stone omen text “great campaign against Cao” was its response.
translations.idiomatic: Jin’s victory over Cao answered the stone motto “punish Cao.”

sentences.zh: 案劉歆以《春秋》石言于晉，為金石同類也，是為金不從革，失其性也，劉向以為石白色為主，屬白祥。

translations.literal: According to Liu Xin, in the Spring and Autumn stone spoke in Jin—stone and metal are of the same kind; this is metal not yielding to change and losing its nature. Liu Xiang took stone’s white color as ruling aspect—belonging to white omens.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xin linked speaking stone to metal’s stubbornness; Liu Xiang read white stone as a white omen.

sentences.zh: 魏明帝青龍中，盛修宮室，西取長安金狄，承露槃折，聲聞數十里，金狄泣，於是因留霸城。

translations.literal: In Wei Mingdi’s Qinglong years palace building flourished greatly; they took metal figures from Chang’an in the west—the dew-collecting basin snapped, sound heard for several tens of li; the metal figures wept; therefore they were left at Ba city.
translations.idiomatic: Mingdi’s builders hauled Chang’an’s bronze figures east; the dew tray broke with a roar; statues seemed to weep—left at Ba.

sentences.zh: 此金失其性而為異也。

translations.literal: This was metal losing its nature and becoming prodigious.
translations.idiomatic: Metal had turned unnatural.

sentences.zh: 吳時，曆陽縣有岩穿，似印，咸云「石印封發，天下太平」。

translations.literal: In Wu times Liyang county had a rock pierced like a seal; all said “when the stone seal opens and issues, all under Heaven is at peace.”
translations.idiomatic: Wu folk saw a seal-shaped pierced rock: “When the stone seal opens, the realm is calm.”

sentences.zh: 孫皓，印發。

translations.literal: Sun Hao—the seal opened.
translations.idiomatic: Under Sun Hao the seal “opened.”

sentences.zh: 又，陽羨山有石穴，長十餘丈。

translations.literal: Moreover Mount Yangxian had a stone cave more than ten zhang long.
translations.idiomatic: Yangxian’s mountain held a ten-zhang cavern.

sentences.zh: 皓初修武昌宮，有遷都之意。

translations.literal: Hao first repaired Wuchang Palace with intent to move the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao rebuilt Wuchang palace—capital-move plans.

sentences.zh: 是時武昌為離宮。

translations.literal: At this time Wuchang was a detached palace.
translations.idiomatic: Wuchang served as a secondary palace.

sentences.zh: 班固云「離宮與城郭同占」，飾城郭之謂也。

translations.literal: Ban Gu said “detached palace shares omen with walls and moats”—this speaks of adorning walls and moats.
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu equates detached palaces with fortifications—showy ramparts.

sentences.zh: 其後，皓出東關，遣丁奉至合肥，皓又大舉出華里，侵邊境之謂也。

translations.literal: Afterward Hao went out East Pass, sent Ding Fei to Hefei; Hao again mounted a great expedition out Huali—this speaks of encroaching borderlands.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hao marched east, sent Ding Fei north—border raids as foretold.

sentences.zh: 故令金失其性，卒面縛而吳亡。

translations.literal: Therefore metal was made to lose its nature; in the end bound facing forward and Wu perished.
translations.idiomatic: Metal’s virtue fled; Sun Hao bound himself and Wu fell.

sentences.zh: 惠帝閏二月，殿前六鐘皆出涕，五刻止。

translations.literal: In Huidi’s intercalary second month the six bells before the hall all issued tears; after five ke they stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Hui: six court bells wept oil five ke long.

sentences.zh: 前年賈后殺楊太后于金墉城，而賈后為惡不止，故鐘出涕，猶傷之也。

translations.literal: The year before Empress Jia killed Empress Dowager Yang at Jinyong Fortress, yet Empress Jia’s evil did not cease—therefore the bells issued tears, still grieving it.
translations.idiomatic: After Jia murdered Yang at Jinyong and kept sinning, the bells wept for her.

sentences.zh: ，成都伐長沙，每夜戈戟鋒有火光如懸燭。

translations.literal: , Chengdu campaigned against Changsha; each night spear and halberd points bore fire-light like hanging candles.
translations.idiomatic: When Chengdu struck Changsha, weapon tips flamed nightly like lamps.

sentences.zh: 此輕人命，好攻戰，金失其性而為光變也。

translations.literal: This was esteeming human lives lightly and loving attack warfare—metal losing its nature and becoming light transformation.
translations.idiomatic: Contempt for life and love of war turned metal into flickering omens.

sentences.zh: 天戒若曰，兵猶火也，不戢將自焚。

translations.literal: Heaven’s warning seemed to say: arms are like fire—if not stowed they will burn oneself.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven warned: armies are fire—unchecked, they consume their masters.

sentences.zh: 成都不悟，終以敗亡。

translations.literal: Chengdu did not awaken and in the end failed and perished.
translations.idiomatic: Chengdu ignored it and fell.

sentences.zh: 懷帝，項縣有魏豫州刺史賈逵石碑，生金可采，此金不從革而為變也。

translations.literal: Under Huaidi Xiang county had Wei Inspector of Yu Province Jia Kui’s stone tablet—it grew harvestable gold—this was metal not yielding to change and becoming prodigy.
translations.idiomatic: A Wei-era stele sprouted workable gold—metal gone strange.

sentences.zh: 五月，汲桑作亂，群寇飆起。

translations.literal: In the fifth month Ji Sang rebelled; bandits rose like a whirlwind.
translations.idiomatic: Fifth month: Ji Sang’s revolt and flying bands.

sentences.zh: 清河王覃為世子時，所佩金鈴忽生起如粟者，康王母疑不祥，毀棄之。

translations.literal: When Prince Qinghe Tan was heir apparent, a golden bell he wore suddenly grew bumps like millet; Prince Kang’s mother deemed it ill-omened and destroyed it.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Tan’s gold bell grew beads like grain—the dowager smashed it as ill luck.

sentences.zh: 及後為惠帝太子，不終於位，卒為司馬越所殺。

translations.literal: Later he became Huidi’s heir but did not finish his tenure; in the end Sima Yue killed him.
translations.idiomatic: Made crown prince, he never succeeded—Sima Yue slew him.

sentences.zh: 湣帝，石言於平陽。

translations.literal: Under Mindi stone spoke at Pingyang.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Min: stone spoke at Pingyang.

sentences.zh: 是時帝蒙塵亦在平陽，故有非言之物而言，妖之大者。

translations.literal: At this time the emperor suffered dust and dishonor also at Pingyang; therefore a thing that should not speak spoke—the greatest of prodigies.
translations.idiomatic: The captive emperor was there—things that cannot speak spoke; dire portent.

sentences.zh: 俄而帝為逆胡所弑。

translations.literal: Soon the emperor was murdered by rebellious Hu.
translations.idiomatic: Soon barbarian rebels murdered him.

sentences.zh: 元帝，甘卓將襲王敦，既而中止。

translations.literal: Under Yuandi Gan Zhuo was about to strike Wang Dun, then stopped midway.
translations.idiomatic: Gan Zhuo planned to strike Wang Dun—then halted.

sentences.zh: 及還，家多變怪，照鏡不見其頭。

translations.literal: When he returned home there were many anomalies; looking in the mirror he did not see his head.
translations.idiomatic: Home filled with marvels; his mirror showed no head.

sentences.zh: 此金失其性而為妖也。

translations.literal: This was metal losing its nature and becoming prodigious.
translations.idiomatic: Metal had turned demonic.

sentences.zh: 尋為敦所襲，遂夷滅。

translations.literal: Soon Dun attacked him and he was exterminated.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun fell on him and wiped him out.

sentences.zh: 石季龍時，鄴城鳳陽門上金鳳皇二頭飛入漳河。

translations.literal: Under Shi Hu two golden phoenix heads on Fengyang Gate at Ye city flew into the Zhang River.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Hu’s reign: Ye’s gate bronze phoenix heads flew into the Zhang.

sentences.zh: 海西太和中，會稽山陰縣起倉，鑿地得兩大船，滿中錢，錢皆輪文大形。
